timeline.text: The prescribed timeline for Building Plan Approval is 15 days, including approximately 3 days for initial processing and 7 days for site inspection; the remaining time covers technical scrutiny, decision-making, fee payment and certificate issuance.

documents: Applicable heritage, land-use, road widening and other statutory clearances (depending on project)
licenses.documentsNote: Several items (Structural Stability Certificate, heritage/land-use/road-widening NOCs) apply only 'where applicable' or 'depending on the project'; exact triggering criteria not specified.

deemedApproval.text: Deemed approval is not applicable for Building Plan Approval in Ladakh; no provision for deemed approval is currently operational in practice.

validity.text: Buildings below 15 metres height: 3 years from the date of sanction. Buildings above 15 metres height: 5 years from the date of sanction.

fees.text: Processed online through OBPS; the commercial building permission fee is ₹109 per sq. metre, paid after approval. No residential fee figure was given.

steps.title: Application Submission
steps.note: Submitted via the OBPS online portal; residential applicants apply directly, commercial applicants through an empanelled architect; architectural drawings and floor plans are uploaded.

steps.title: Initial Processing
steps.note: Application remains at the initial stage for approximately 3 days before being forwarded to the technical team.

steps.title: Technical Scrutiny
steps.note: Examined by an architect, civil engineer and structural engineer for compliance with bye-laws covering design, setbacks, fire safety and road/highway considerations.

steps.title: Site Inspection
steps.note: Conducted within approximately 7 days, involving municipal enforcement personnel.

steps.title: Scrutiny/Decision
steps.note: Application is either rejected with reasons communicated to the applicant, or forwarded to the Executive Officer for approval.

steps.title: Approval by Executive Officer
steps.note: Executive Officer takes the final decision; the approval is digitally signed.

steps.title: Fee Payment
steps.note: Applicant receives an online notification and pays the building permission fee through the online system.

steps.title: Issuance of Building Permission
steps.note: Building permission certificate is issued online after payment.

remarks: Approximately 50 Building Plan Approval applications had been received during the year up to the date of the discussion; of these, 35 were certified, 7 rejected, and 4 under process.
No specific state-level best practice was reported; however, the OBPS-based online application, tracking and digital certificate issuance may be considered a replicable practice.

Risk-based classification is incorporated in the applicable building bye-laws, including classification of low-risk buildings; further assessment may be undertaken to determine whether this can be leveraged for simplified scrutiny, reduced documentation or faster processing.

findings.text: Applications are submitted through the OBPS online portal; residential applicants can apply directly, while commercial applicants must apply through an empanelled architect.
Two rounds of scrutiny may create additional processing requirements and could be simplified.
Multiple documents and drawings are required to be uploaded through OBPS, creating compliance requirements for applicants.
Minor issues with online payment were reported, which may occasionally affect completion of the approval process.
The inspection/scrutiny stage generally takes comparatively more time within the overall 15-day prescribed timeline.

If an application is rejected, the applicant is informed through OBPS of the reason, may rectify deficiencies and resubmit, and the prescribed 15-day timeline starts afresh from the date of resubmission.
Officials recommended reviewing the 2025 building bye-laws and considering the 2024 bye-laws with necessary changes.
It was suggested that bye-laws account for Ladakh's geographical conditions, plot sizes, fire requirements and local settlement patterns.
Suitable relaxation was recommended for existing buildings in newly included municipal areas.
Officials recommended promoting sustainable construction, local materials and traditional architecture.
Expanding the empanelment of architects was recommended to widen participation and improve accessibility, particularly for commercial building applications.

Risk-based classification is incorporated in the applicable building bye-laws, including classification of low-risk buildings; further assessment may determine whether this enables simplified scrutiny or faster processing.
The OBPS-based online application, tracking and digital certificate issuance was noted as a potentially replicable practice.
Technical scrutiny involves an architect, civil engineer and structural engineer reviewing compliance with building bye-laws covering design, setbacks, fire safety and road/highway considerations.
Approximately 50 BPA applications were received in the year to date; 35 certified, 7 rejected and 4 under process at the time of the discussion.
No specific post-approval compliance checklist was identified beyond the validity period of the building permission.
Validity of the building permission is 3 years for buildings below 15 metres and 5 years for buildings above 15 metres, from the date of sanction.

gaps.text: No URL is given for the OBPS portal.

Several documentation items (Structural Stability Certificate, heritage/land-use/road-widening NOCs) apply only 'where applicable' or 'depending on the project', without the specific triggering criteria being stated.
The OBPS single-window online system with digital tracking and digital certificate issuance was flagged by officials as a replicable practice for other states.
Officials suggested simplifying the technical scrutiny process to reduce duplication from the two rounds of scrutiny (technical review and site inspection/decision).
Only the commercial building fee (₹109 per sq. metre) is given; no residential fee figure is stated.

Of the 15-day total timeline, only the initial ~3 days and ~7-day inspection are broken out; the remaining time for technical scrutiny, decision, fee payment and certificate issuance is not individually apportioned.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Fire & Rescue Service, UT-Ladakh; final Fire NOC issued by the designated authority (e.g., District Fire Officer/Deputy Director)

timeline.basis: Departmental processing timeline as indicated by officials; an additional 20-day period may apply after rejection and resubmission
timeline.text: The department has indicated an application processing timeline of 20 days. In case of rejection and resubmission, an additional 20-day period may apply.

licenses.documentsNote: These documents are specified for the provisional Fire NOC application; no separate document list is given for the final Fire NOC application after construction.

deemedApproval.text: A deemed approval provision of 21 days was discussed; however, its current operational status requires clarification.

validity.text: Validity varies by building category: Category 1 (Residential) - 1 year under earlier practice; Category 2 (self-certification by empanelled architects) - 10 years, with a return submitted every 2 years; Category 3 (other, including Commercial and Industrial) - 5 years, with an annual return requirement.

fees.text: The earlier application fee for the provisional Fire NOC was ₹1,000; following proposed fee deregulation, the Fire NOC application fee in Ladakh is now nil (free of charge).

steps.title: Application Submission (Provisional Fire NOC)
steps.note: Submitted through the existing departmental process or the e-Seva portal, where available.

steps.title: Document Submission
steps.note: Applicant submits building plan, site plan and required fire safety drawings.

steps.title: Fee Payment
steps.note: Applicant pays the applicable fee as per prevailing instructions (now nil after fee deregulation).

steps.title: Application Scrutiny
steps.note: Fire Department examines submitted documents and verifies the building category against the applicable schedule.

steps.title: Provisional NOC
steps.note: Department reviews the application and issues the provisional recommendation/NOC, wherever applicable, before construction.

steps.title: Completion of Construction / Final Application
steps.note: After completing construction, the applicant applies for the final Fire NOC.

steps.title: Inspection Scheduling
steps.note: Fire Department arranges an inspection by the District Fire Officer (DFO) or an empanelled third-party agency, as applicable.

steps.title: Site Inspection
steps.note: Designated officer or agency inspects the building to verify compliance with fire safety requirements.

steps.title: Inspection Report Submission
steps.note: Inspection report is submitted to the concerned authority for review.

steps.title: Review and Approval
steps.note: Concerned authority reviews the inspection report and processes the application for final approval.

steps.title: Fire NOC Issuance
steps.note: Upon approval, the final Fire NOC is issued by the designated authority.

ed.location: DIC Office Complex, DIC Conference Hall, Near Court Complex, Skampari, Leh, Ladakh

remarks: The Fire NOC service in Ladakh is currently undergoing a transition to the single-window system; implementation of the 2025 Fire NOC rules, the online application workflow and third-party inspection provisions is still being clarified.
Coordination between the Fire Department and other concerned authorities also requires further clarification to ensure smooth implementation of the revised procedures.
No specific best practice for replication in other States/UTs was identified during the discussion.

findings.text: The Fire NOC service is currently partially online as transition to the single-window system is underway; registration, document upload, fee payment and status tracking are available via the e-Seva portal where operational, while scrutiny, inspection and approval remain largely offline/departmental.

The requirement for third-party inspection may add to the compliance burden and increase costs for applicants; allowing the Fire Department to conduct inspections as an alternative could reduce additional expenses and simplify the approval process.

In remote areas, availability of water and fire safety equipment may create additional compliance challenges for maintaining required fire safety infrastructure (extinguishers, sprinklers, water storage/tanks, pumps, alarms).

The transition to the new Fire NOC framework has created ambiguity regarding the roles of the department and third-party agencies; clarifying procedures and responsibilities could reduce procedural delays and duplication.
The exact financial savings and reduction in processing time from the proposed reforms have not been quantified in the discussion.
Specific provisions of the Central Act or State Rules responsible for the compliance burdens described were not clearly identified during the discussion.
It was suggested the Fire Department retain the option to conduct inspections directly alongside empanelled third-party agencies to reduce additional compliance costs.
A standard operating procedure (SOP) clarifying the roles and responsibilities of the department and third-party agencies was suggested to simplify the approval process and reduce procedural delays.
Providing suitable timelines for inspections in remote areas of Ladakh was suggested, to address challenges from limited road connectivity and winter conditions.
Following proposed fee deregulation, the Fire NOC application fee in Ladakh is now nil, down from an earlier fee of ₹1,000.
Buildings are categorised by occupancy, number of rooms, height and covered area into three categories, with Category 1 (1-14 rooms) exempt from regular Fire NOC requirements.
Category 2 buildings (15-30 rooms) permit self-certification by empanelled architects, while Category 3 (above 30 rooms) requires third-party inspection.

Validity differs by category: 1 year for residential (earlier practice), 10 years with a return every 2 years for self-certified buildings, and 5 years with annual return for commercial/industrial buildings.
A deemed approval provision of 21 days was discussed, but its current operational status requires clarification.
No specific best practice for replication in other States/UTs was identified during the discussion.
Coordination between the Fire Department and other concerned authorities requires further clarification to ensure smooth implementation of revised procedures.
In case of rejection and resubmission of the Fire NOC application, an additional 20-day processing period may apply.

gaps.text: A deemed approval provision of 21 days was discussed but its current operational status (active or not) is unclear.
The complete online workflow and third-party inspection procedures are described as 'still being clarified', without specifying what is settled versus pending.
No specific name/designation of the 'designated authority' issuing the final Fire NOC is given beyond general department roles (DFO, IC NOC, Deputy Director).

Documentation requirements are given only for the provisional NOC stage (building plan, site plan, fire safety drawings); no document list is given for the final Fire NOC application submitted after construction.
Officials suggested allowing the Fire Department to conduct inspections directly as an alternative to third-party agencies, to reduce compliance costs and administrative burden.
The exact financial savings and reduction in processing time from the proposed reforms were not quantified in the discussion.
Specific provisions of the Central Act or State Rules responsible for the described compliance burdens were not clearly identified during the discussion.
